replying_to: Replying to Learning Multi-Objective Curricula for Deep Reinforcement Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper1952 by Reviewer iZmE

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a curriculum reinforcement learning method that fuses multiple curriculum paradigms into a neural network architecture. More precisely, curricula over startings states, goal states and reward shaping functions are realized by recurrent neural networks parameterized by a hyper network. Additionally, the authors experiment with what they refer to as an abstract curriculum. This curriculum is realized as an additional memory mechanism from which the agent reads additional information. This additional information is aimed at improving the agents learning performance. The hypernetwork is trained simultaneously to the RL agent by minimizing various Bellmann errors.

The authors provide experimental evidence that their proposed way of learning curricula can improve the performance compared to baseline automated curriculum reinforcement learning methods in the CausalWorld environment suite.
content.main_review:
Before stating my review I want to disclose that I already reviewed this paper for another conference. However, I do not know about the identity of the authors as the paper has not been accepted back then. At the previous conference, the paper was rejected e.g. because a lack of baseline comparisons, untangible experimental results and a suboptimal presentation of the method.

In general, I see that the paper has been improved substantially w.r.t. baseline comparisons and the presentation of experimental results. Also the presentation of the method has been improved. Nonetheless, I still see potential for improving the clarity of the presentation:

* The objectives for the individual curricula seem to use Q-functions with different inputs. For the subgoal curriculum, an additional input $c_{goal}$ is added. For the initial state curriculum, this sub-goal is, however, missing in the objective. The abstract curriculum then again uses a Q-function defined over the abstract curriculum output $c_{abs}$ but not incorporating $c_{goal}$. This raises questions about the form of the Q function that the agent is using. Is it defined over all the previously mentioned inputs?
* Does the goal state generated by the subgoal module influence the reward function? Unfortunately, this seems to be not discussed.
* In the last version of the paper, the authors discussed that the abstract curriculum module needs to be pre-trained on some related tasks before being used. In the experimental section of this version, this discussion is not included anymore. Did the authors find a way to avoid this form of pre-training or is it still necessary? In the latter case, the authors should describe this pre-training.
* The pick-and-place task as a comparison w.r.t. to ALP-GMM and GoalGAN seems to be missing. Is this a mistake or are there reasons why this task is missing for the baseline comparisons but present for the ablations?

Apart from the issues w.r.t. presentation and clarity of the paper, I have additional conceptual questions:

* Given that the memory mechanism is write-only for the hyper network, shouldn't it be possible to just directly predict the abstract curriculum information $c_{abs}$ instead of reading it from a memory? Theoretically, the recurrent nature of the hyper network should already allow to realize a form of memory. Maybe an ablation of this external memory could shed additional light on its importance on the performance.
* Is the reward shaping curriculum allowed to change the shaping function in each environment step of the agent training? In this case, it may not be in line with the theoretical framework by Ng et al. To clarify: This question came up in the last review during the reviewer discussion so that the authors did not have a chance to answer to this question back then.
* Finally, I am missing a motivation why the Bellmann error is a suitable objective for training the hyper network. How does it relate to optimizing the agent performance? I am asking because being able to correctly encode the expected policy performance by minimizing a Bellmann error does not necessarily mean that the corresponding policy achieves high expected returns. Consequently, a discussion of this objective would improve the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: In general, I think the paper is an encouraging work. However, the still many questions w.r.t. clarity and concept of the paper do not allow me to say that this work is very close to the acceptance threshold. Nonetheless, I think that many of my questions can be addressed in a revised version during the rebuttal. If this is the case, I am happy to improve my score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iZmE (2)
content.comment:
>Q: Finally, I am missing a motivation why the Bellmann error is a suitable objective for training the hyper network. How does it relate to optimizing the agent performance? I am asking because being able to correctly encode the expected policy performance by minimizing a Bellmann error does not necessarily mean that the corresponding policy achieves high expected returns. Consequently, a discussion of this objective would improve the paper.

R: We would like to emphasize that our curriculum generator (i.e., Hyper-RNN) is trained in a well-established framework of meta RL following [Meta-Q-Learning] [Discovering Reinforcement Learning Algorithms] [Learning to Reinforcement Learn]. The Hyper-RNN is "meta-trained" on a large number of different tasks (e.g., reaching, picking), and aims to adapt to a new task quickly by providing useful curricula to the inner-loop RL agent. The key concept is that the Hyper-RNN controls the **learning progress** of the Base-RNN in the inner loop, but not just the final Bellman loss for a particular inner-loop. In other words, Hyper-RNN learns how to generate a series of progressive goals and initial states for the Base-RNN, **across multiple inner loops**, and the memory mechanism of the Hyper-RNN can maintain such information. 

If the Hyper-RNN generates some easy initial states or goal states, they may not necessarily help the inner-loop Base-RNN to achieve good performance in a new environment after convergence. Thus, the key is not to generate too easy or too hard curricula, but a series of suitable curricula across multiple inner loops. 

Furthermore, since our framework can propose multiple curricula without conflicts, it is at least robust than using a single curriculum, which has been thoroughly investigated in our experiments.

The motivations of using Bellman error can be also concluded in the followings:

First, we link the hyper-RNN parameter training to the policy learning so that we can optimize the hyper-RNN parameter in the meta reinforcement learning framework. Specifically, the actor-network and critic network are inner loop parameters optimization. The outer loop is to optimize the hyper-RNN parameter training. By adding the outputs of base-RNNs to the Q function, we manage to combine the inner training and outer training together.

Second, by adding curricula to the Q function, we plan to have a better estimation of the generated curricula based on the current state and action. In actor-critic learning algorithms, the Q value function plays as guidance for the policy parameters optimization. It acts like controlling the direction and how far the parameters should be updated in the next step. Thus, learning a better Q value function helps agents search for a good policy and receive better rewards.

We are happy to answer any other questions you may have.

content.title: The accompanying code is problematic
content.comment:
After reading the authors’ responses to my questions and being still unsure about the pre-training of the hyper networks (which is now mentioned only vaguely), the reward shaping and the use of the bellman error as guiding the curriculum generation, I decided to take a look at the accompanying code of the paper, as I could not reply to the authors before the rebuttal deadline and hence wanted to take an honest effort in resolving my remaining questions without further input from the authors.

However, this investigation revealed several problems that prevent me for recommending anything else than rejection of the paper. I will detail the issues now (in increasing severity):

*  I could not find any code for the only vaguely mentioned pre-training. In **src/train_causal_world.py**, there is only a **load_dir** parameter that, however, causes the only the policy to load previously saved parameters. The parameter for the curriculum modules are not loaded at all.
* Opposing the statement of the authors, the **shaping reward DOES change** throughout execution of a policy and hence **does not fulfill the conditions by Ng et al** [1]. This can be seen in the **collect_rollouts** method in **src/core/custom_on_policy_algorithm.py** (line 190-197), where the state and hyper_state variables that are used for the prediction of the shaping reward are updated with every step in the environment. Hence the reward shaping potential does no stay consistent throughout a trajectory. Further, I realized that even if the reward shaping potential stayed the same, the authors use $\gamma F(\mathbf{s}') - F(\mathbf{s})$ as the shaping reward, where $\gamma$ is, however, **not** equal to the discounting factor of the environment. However, this needs to be the case as e.g. stated in Theorem 1 of [1].
* The individual curriculum mechanisms do not seem to be combined in the way they are described in the paper. Looking again at the **collect_rollouts** method of the **src/core/custom_on_policy_training.py**, we see in lines 202-209 that the memory of the abstract curriculum module is not passed at all to the policy, if also the subgoal curriculum is active. The same is the case for the **outer_loss** and **train** methods in **src/core/custom_ppo.py** (lines 185-194 and lines 276-285). Hence, it is questionable what effect the abstract curriculum should have, it the policy is not consuming any information from this module.
* Finally, the **loss functions described in the paper seem to be not used for training the hyper RNN**. In the **outer_loss** function in **src/core/custom_ppo.py**, the regular loss of the PPO algorithm is used (line 230/231) for training the hyper RNN instead of the reported bellman errors. It would anyways be questionable, how the update should use the reported bellman errors, as the errors rely on a Q-function, which PPO does not estimate by default. Additionally, it seems that only an optimizer object for the goal generation module is instantiated in the **train** function of **src/core/custom_ppo.py** (line 256) that then updates the parameters of this module in line 368. This made me curious, whether the parameters of the reward shaping- and initial state module were changed at all via training and hence I ran the **train_causal_world.py** script to compare the parameter values after some iterations of the algorithm (I needed to fix an error for that as I describe in the next point). The result: **None of the parameters of the curriculum modules have been updated during training**. While I was expecting this for the reward shaping- and initial state module (as I could not find any optimizers instantiated for those), I was surprised that this was the case for the goal generation module. Checking the **reverse_unroll** method that is called in the **train** method in **src/core/custom_ppo.py**, it turned out the returned gradients were always None. Maybe this is because of a disconnected computation graph.
* As mentioned, I could not run the training without fixing an issue that cause an Exception first. The problem is that the **reverse_unroll** method in the **train** method of **src/core/custom_ppo.py** is given a generator object (self.hparams) which after being used once, only returns an empty list. Hence, the torch.autograd.grad call fails on the second invocation of the **reverse_unroll** method, as the generator object is empty by that time.

These issues do not allow me to recommend acceptance of the paper, as the disconnect between paper and accompanying code is definitely too large and the code further seems to contain severe issues. Hence to me, the validity of the results is questionable.

content.title: Problems still seem to persist
content.comment:
I thank the authors for the link to the GitHub repository with the more recent code. While the individual curriculum module outputs now seem to be combined in the way described in the paper, my other concerns still persist after looking at the more up-to-date code:

* Loading of the pre-trained curriculum modules, while now loading the hyper net and curriculum module parameters, still also loads the policy parameters (https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/train_causal_world.py#L124). Does that mean that the pre-training of the curriculum also implicitly pre-trains the policy?
* The reward shaping module, while defined as the subtraction as a potential function evaluated at two subsequent states $\gamma F(s’) - F(s)$, does not fulfill the properties defined by Ng et al. in order to leave the optimal policy invariant. The problem arises because the potential $F(\cdot)$ is assumed to be fixed during a trajectory by Ng et al. Actually, it may be even assumed to be fixed throughout the complete training of the RL agent but it becomes obvious that it needs to be fixed for one trajectory rollout when following the sufficiency proof on page 5 of this (http://luthuli.cs.uiuc.edu/~daf/courses/games/AIpapers/ml99-shaping.pdf) document. However, as can be seen in the collect_rollouts method (https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/core/custom_on_policy_algorithm.py#L225), the (hyper-)LSTM state changes with each environment step. As this also changes the shaping potential, the assumptions of Ng et al are not fulfilled (in addition to the mismatch in the discounting term that I already mentioned).
* The loss function for the curriculum module training (https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/core/custom_ppo.py#L315) is still the PPO loss and not a TD-Error of a $Q$-function. The authors linked to https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/core/custom_ppo.py#L306, where the „value-loss“ part of the PPO objective is defined. However, as can be seen in line 315 (see link above), the full loss also incorporates the policy loss and entropy loss of the PPO objective.
* I did not re-verify the issue with the **None** values for the new code. However, the authors still only initialize and use an optimizer object for the subgoal module (https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/core/custom_ppo.py#L341 and https://github.com/6148Authours/MOC/blob/7f198a19fc340e50d1033a3724c3227b0c8e9b4b/src/core/custom_ppo.py#L459), but not for any of the other curriculum modules. 

Consequently, I still see obvious differences between the described approach and the evaluated implementation.

content.comment:
We are extremely appreciative of your endeavor to check our research code. We'd hope you could understand that we've always been trying our best to make our results reproducible. We will later make it cleaner.

Does that mean that the pre-training of the curriculum also implicitly pre-trains the policy?

R: We do **NOT** pre-train the policy when pre-training the "abstract" curriculum. The codes here illustrate the API **how** we import the pre-trained model, which is not the way we pre-train the "abstract" curriculum. We thank you for asking and we will complete all APIs when we open-source our codes.

>Q: The reward shaping module, while defined as the subtraction as a potential function evaluated at two subsequent states, does not fulfill the properties defined by Ng et al. in order to leave the optimal policy invariant. The problem arises because the potential is assumed to be fixed during a trajectory by Ng et al. Actually, it may be even assumed to be fixed throughout the complete training of the RL agent but it becomes obvious that it needs to be fixed for one trajectory rollout when following the sufficiency proof on page 5 of this (http://luthuli.cs.uiuc.edu/~daf/courses/games/AIpapers/ml99-shaping.pdf) document. R: Thank you for pointing this out. The reason why the shaping function $F(\cdot)$ is unchanged is that we do not change the generated reward curriculum parameters in each time step. However, we argue that changing the hyper-RNN states has very limited effects on the reward curriculum. Besides, we emphasize that our major contribution is learning multi-objective curricula through the bi-level optimization framework. 

In order to demonstrate the significance of changing hyper-RNN states, we fixed the hyper-RNN states and evaluated their performance. Specifically, we tested on two methods, which are MOC and MOC with reward curriculum only (denoted as MOC_{reward+, memory-}). The results are shown below. As we can see in this table, we do not find any significant affections of whether fix the hyper-RNN state. We are also running experiments on other tasks and will keep updating the new results.

content.title: Final Answer
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their effort. Indeed, the answer addressed my previous concerns, however, there are yet additional questions raised. While I will state them here (to give the authors indications for improvement), I will not change my score as I believe that the paper needs a proper re-writing to reflect the actual method and further, the code needs to be cleaned up and the experiments potentially re-run with the proper code:

* The experimental insights regarding the reward shaping are interesting and empirically motivate why the proposed method still works despite not being in line with the strict theory of Ng et al. However, the authors need to state that their way of generating the shaping potential deviates from the theory to avoid misconceptions
* I agree with the authors that the policy and entropy loss do not influence the gradients for the shared hypernet as the policy is only given the non-augmented observations from the environment. This, however, raises two questions:
1. Why are theses losses computed in the first place? I agree that research code does not need to be cleaned up perfectly, but computing unused quantities raises doubts about the care being taken in the investigation of the proposed method, even if the authors may have actually taken the required amount of care.
2. More importantly, the differing inputs to the value function and policy raise another theoretical issues. First, in the paper, the authors describe that they are working with $Q$-functions to compute the TD-errors instead of the value functions used in the actual code. Second, I think that from a theoretical perspective, the motivation of adding additional inputs only to the value function but not the policy requires additional clarification. Given that the value function is defined as $V(s) = E_{a \sim \pi(s)} \left[ r(s, a) + \gamma E_{s' \sim p(s, a)}\left[V(s')\right]\right]$, the policy is typically defined on the same inputs as the value function. Hence, readers (just as me) would assume that this is the case in your method as well, as omitting inputs that characterize the current task (such as the desired goal to be reached) typically make learning more complicated due to partial observability. Why did the authors choose to not extend the input of the policy? This question should be clearly discussed in the main paper.

>Q: Why are these losses computed in the first place? I agree that the research code does not need to be cleaned up perfectly, but computing unused quantities raise doubts about the care being taken in the investigation of the proposed method, even if the authors may have actually taken the required amount of care.

R: The implementation here shows how MOC can be easily applied to existing actor-critic algorithms. To use our proposed MOC framework, the minor modification to the critic loss functions is well enough. Because there are no gradients back-propagated, which do not harm the hyper-RNN training.

>Q: More importantly, the differing inputs to the value function and policy raise another theoretical issues. First, in the paper, the authors describe that they are working with functions to compute the TD-errors instead of the value functions used in the actual code. 

R: The "value loss" implemented in the code base is not value functions. We actually do compute the TD-errors ****as our value loss. A value function cannot ****be a loss ****for the training. Moreover, the TD-errors do require computing the value functions**,** which may potentially cause the misleading here.

>Q: Second, I think that from a theoretical perspective, the motivation of adding additional inputs only to the value function but not the policy requires additional clarification. Given that the value function is defined as the policy is typically defined on the same inputs as the value function. Hence, readers (just as me) would assume that this is the case in your method as well, as omitting inputs that characterize the current task (such as the desired goal to be reached) typically make learning more complicated due to partial observability. Why did the authors choose to not extend the input of the policy? This question should be clearly discussed in the main paper.

R: Using additional inputs to the value function is inspired by universal value functions [1], which is explained in the main paper Sec3.1 paragraph 2 "To incorporate the subgoal state in the overall computation graph, in this paper, we adopt the idea from universal value functions".

However, we do not see any other papers that describe the same combination in policy functions.

More importantly, the implementation of policy functions usually makes use of the reparameterization trick. The action is sampled from a distribution instead of directly generated from Neural Networks, which causes no-gradient when adding inputs to policy functions. 

We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. Due to the page limit, we did not put this discussion in the main paper. We will add this clarification in the Appendix.

[1] Schaul, T., Horgan, D., Gregor, K., & Silver, D. (2015). Universal Value Function Approximators. *ICML*.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iZmE (1)
content.comment:
Thanks for your constructive suggestions and here are our responses to your questions. We also revised our paper according to your comments, which are shown in red violet text.

> Q: The objectives for the individual curricula seem to use Q-functions with different inputs. For the subgoal curriculum, an additional input cgoal is added. For the initial state curriculum, this sub-goal is, however, missing in the objective. The abstract curriculum then again uses a Q-function defined over the abstract curriculum output cabs but not incorporating cgoal. This raises questions about the form of the Q function that the agent is using. Is it defined over all the previously mentioned inputs?

R: In the paper, we divide the Q function in terms of different curricula to clearly demonstrate how we design loss functions for each curriculum. As for the implementation, we combine all the loss function terms and set them as inputs to the Q-function. Thank you for the suggestion, and we've revised this part in the paper (Sec. 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 in red text) to make it more clear. 

> Q: Does the goal state generated by the subgoal module influence the reward function? Unfortunately, this seems to be not discussed.

R: The Base-RNN components are independent for each curriculum and don't affect each other. This means the goal state subgoal module doesn't influence the reward function module. 

> Q: In the last version of the paper, the authors discussed that the abstract curriculum module needs to be pre-trained on some related tasks before being used. In the experimental section of this version, this discussion is not included anymore. Did the authors find a way to avoid this form of pre-training or is it still necessary? In the latter case, the authors should describe this pre-training.

R: We still pre-train the abstract memory module. We have added this description to Appendix Sec. A.8. To ensure that the pre-training does not provide extra information pertaining to the target training tasks, we pre-train the abstract memory module in an irrelevant task. 
That is, when solving task X, we pre-train the abstract memory module on tasks other than X. Details can be found in our source code.

> Q: The pick-and-place task as a comparison w.r.t. to ALP-GMM and GoalGAN seems to be missing. Is this a mistake or are there reasons why this task is missing for the baseline comparisons but present for the ablations?

R: We apologize for not showing these results in the paper due to the page limit. We've added it to Appendix Fig.11.

> Q: Given that the memory mechanism is write-only for the hyper network, shouldn't it be possible to just directly predict the abstract curriculum information cabs instead of reading it from a memory? Theoretically, the recurrent nature of the hyper network should already allow to realize a form of memory. Maybe an ablation of this external memory could shed additional light on its importance on the performance.

R: We have conducted additional experiments as you suggested. As can be seen below, direct-memory is somewhat useful, but MOC still outperforms it. One possible reason might be that when the agent reads messages from the memory, the agent will attend to the vector, which is different from the direct-memory. This is explained in Sec. 3.2.

|       Algorithms | Reaching | Picking | Stacking | Pick and place| Pushing |
|:---------------------------:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
|    $MOC_{base-} $  |  596.02+/-178.90  | -15.56+/-1.79 | -10.09+/-2.36 | -8.68+-2.27 | -8.68+-2.27 |
|        Direct Memory       |  543.68+/-239.71  | -17.99+/-2.15 | -15.73+/-5.07 | -13.04+-2.00 | -9.69+-3.69 |

> Q: Is the reward shaping curriculum allowed to change the shaping function in each environment step of the agent training? In this case, it may not be in line with the theoretical framework by Ng et al. To clarify: This question came up in the last review during the reviewer discussion so that the authors did not have a chance to answer to this question back then.

R: This is in line with the theoretical framework by Ng et al. The shaping function doesn't change in the policy training (inner loop) step because it is generated from Hyper-RNN whose parameters are fixed in the policy (inner loop) training. However, when optimizing the Hyper-RNN in the outer loop, in which we fix the policy parameters, the shaping function will change and be applied to the next policy training steps.

- The proposed method consistently outperforms the GoalGAN and ALP-GMM baselines in the CasualWorld environment.

- The authors provide a detailed ablation study to discuss the importance of each module in the proposed framework.

Weaknesses:

- Could the authors provide a concrete definition and some intuitions to explain the latent curriculum information in Sec. 3.2? It is a bit confusing what the hyper-Net aims to learn to capture. It would be even better if the authors could visualize such curriculum information in the latent space in the experiments.

- In Sec. 3.1 the authors describe that the base-RNN can be used for shaping the rewards. However, there is no experiment demonstrating the generated reward function or how reward shaping helps improve performance. It would be better if the authors could provide qualitative results as well as an ablation study. 

- It is surprising that the random baseline achieves a 90% success rate in Sec. 4.4, which is significantly better than GoalGAN and ALP-GMM. Could the authors explain why that is the case? Given these results, I believe it would be necessary to also include a Random baseline for the subgoal curriculum and incorporate its curve in Figure 2. Without such comparisons, it would be hard to justify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Fq4s
content.comment:
Thanks for your constructive suggestions and here are our responses to your questions. We also revised our paper according to your comments, shown in sky blue text. 
> Q: More baselines are needed. Currently, the method only compares with GoalGAN(Florensa et al. 18) and ALP-GMM (Portelas et al., 19). There are some simpler baselines missing: PPO with a single curriculum such as adapting initial state [1], or reward shaping [2].

R: Thank you for the suggestions. We've added InitialGAN[1] and PPO with reward shaping in the Appendix Fig. 13.

> Q: The robustness of the proposed curricula is unclear. The curricula for generating sub-goals and initial states aim to find goals or initial states where bellman loss is low, indicating that the agent has mastered the states. However, in the extreme case, the network can learn to generate curricula where the sub-goals are too easy to achieve or the initial states are too easy. It is not clear how robust the current method is to such cases.

R: We would like to emphasize that our curriculum generator (i.e., Hyper-RNN) is trained in a well-established framework of meta RL following [Meta-Q-Learning] [Discovering Reinforcement Learning Algorithms] [Learning to Reinforcement Learn]. The Hyper-RNN is "meta-trained" on a large number of different tasks (e.g., reaching, picking), and aims to adapt to a new task quickly by providing useful curricula to the inner-loop RL agent. The key concept is that the Hyper-RNN controls the **learning progress** of the Base-RNN in the inner loop, but not just the final Bellman loss for a particular inner-loop. In other words, Hyper-RNN learns how to generate a series of progressive goals and initial states for the Base-RNN, **across multiple inner loops**, and the memory mechanism of the Hyper-RNN can maintain such information. 
If the Hyper-RNN generates some easy initial states or goal states, they may not necessarily help the inner-loop Base-RNN to achieve good performance in a new environment after convergence. Thus, the key is not to generate too easy or too hard curricula, but a series of suitable curricula across multiple inner loops. 
Furthermore, since our framework can propose multiple curricula without conflicts, it is at least robust than using a single curriculum, which has been thoroughly investigated in our experiments.

The motivation of using Bellman error can be also concluded in two folds:

(1) We link the hyper-RNN parameter training to the policy learning so that we can optimize the hyper-RNN parameter in the meta reinforcement learning framework. Specifically, the actor-network and critic network are inner loop parameters optimization. The outer loop is to optimize the hyper-RNN parameter training. By adding the outputs of base-RNNs to the Q function, we manage to combine the inner training and outer training together.

(2) by adding curricula to the Q function, we plan to have a better estimation of the generated curricula based on the current state and action. In actor-critic learning algorithms, the Q value function plays as guidance for the policy parameters optimization. It acts like controlling the direction and how far the parameters should be updated in the next step. Thus, learning a better Q value function helps agents search for a good policy and receive better rewards.

> Q: Sec. 3.1 described the training objectives in terms of a Q function, but PPO is used in the experiments. How is PPO adapted to learn with Q function?

R: PPO is an actor-critic method and we apply the objectives of Q function as the critic function. 
We have made this clear in our revised document in Appendix Sec. A5.

> Q: How does Q function take in a sequence of sub-goals as input?

R: The Q function takes one subgoal as its input instead of a sequence of sub-goals. In this paper, we applied average pooling for the generated subgoal sequence. We also added this clarification in **Sec. 3.1**.

> Q: In Sec. 3.3, how to alternate between the outer level optimization and the inner level optimization?

R: **Step 1** Update PPO agent parameters $\theta$ on one sampled task by Eqn 3.

**Step 2** With updated parameters $\theta$, we train model parameters $\theta_h$ via SGD by minimizing the  outer loss function $\theta_h^* = argmin_{\theta_h}\mathcal{J}_{outer}$.

**Step 3** With $\theta_h$, we generate manually designed curricula and abstract curriculum.

**Step 4** We give the generated curriculum to the $Q$ function and environment hyper-parameters.

**Step 5** We go back to **Step 1** for agent training until converge.

The detailed explanation is also described in Appendix A.6.

> Q: Notations Sec. 2 are explained in a minimal way and are not self-explanatory.

R: Thank you for the suggestion. Due to the page limit, we've added a section to explain these concepts in Appendix A.7.

We are happy to answer any other questions you may have.

content.title: Follow-up questions
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their responses. Some of my concerns are properly addressed. As some of the details are clarified in the revised version of the paper, I have some follow-up questions:

1. Why are the sub-goals produced from base-RNN averaged? Also, does the super-script of the sub-goal indicates the episode index as in algorithm 1, or the time step within a sequence so that they act like way points? Notation t seems to be overloaded without any explanation.

2. Instead of vanilla PPO,  the paper uses a Q function trained with an entropy regulation term (Eqn. 1). What is the motivation behind that? Additionally, have the authors considered soft actor-critic (Haarnoja et al. 18)?

3. On the motivation of using the bellman loss, I am starting to see the justificaiton of this. Can the authors clarify whether a new environment is sampled each time in the outer loop? This is not mentioned in algorithm 1. 

> The Hyper-RNN is "meta-trained" on a large number of different tasks (e.g., reaching, picking), and aims to adapt to a new task quickly by providing useful curricula to the inner-loop RL agent.

This is very confusing. Is the hyper-RNN trained on all tasks simutaneously? The paper should make it clear what are the distribution of the training and evaluation tasks and how are they sampled in the outer loop.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Fq4s Follow-up questions
content.comment:
>Q: Why are the sub-goals produced from base-RNN averaged? Also, does the super-script of the sub-goal indicates the episode index as in algorithm 1, or the time step within a sequence so that they act like way points? Notation t seems to be overloaded without any explanation.

R: Actually, there are many ways of obtaining the embedding of a sequence of sub-goals. One may even choose to train an RNN over the sequence, and the hidden state vector of the RNN in the last time-step can serve as the embedding of the sub-goal sequence. On the other hand, a simple but effective way is to perform `average pooling`, e.g., exponentially weighted pooling. Actually, in our implementation, we use the most simple form of average pooling — we put all the weight mass on the final sub-goal and zero weights on all the previous sub-goals. In other words, we only use the last sub-goal, which works well in practice. The actual implementation of this part can be seen in "custom_on_policy_algorithm.py", line 277.

The notation regarding training step $t$ representing the inner loop and episode $t'$ representing the outer loop is consistent throughout our draft. We first introduce the training step $t$ used for RL agent in the first paragraph of Section 2 and then introduce the episode $t'$ used for automatic curriculum learning in the second paragraph of Section 2. We use the same notation in Algorithm 1. We emphasized this notation in the fourth paragraph, Section 3:

> In our case, the outer-level optimization comes from the curriculum generation loop where each step is an episode denoted as $t'$. On the other hand, the inner-level optimization involves a common DRL agent training loop on the interactions between the environment and the DRL agent, where each time-step at this level is denoted as $t$.
> 

>Q: Instead of vanilla PPO, the paper uses a Q function trained with an entropy regulation term (Eqn. 1). What is the motivation behind that? Additionally, have the authors considered soft actor-critic (Haarnoja et al. 18)?

R: First, MOC is independent of the particular choice of the RL algorithm. 

Second, though MOC can work with vanilla PPO, we find that using the Q function with an entropy term achieves better empirical results consistently. That is, to better estimate the Q function, we adopt the Q function estimation method from standard soft actor-critic (Haarnoja et al. 18). The motivation of the entropy term is the clipped double-Q trick, which takes the minimum Q-value between the two Q approximators.

Please note that all the curriculum learning methods are evaluated based on the same RL algorithm. 

>Q: On the motivation of using the bellman loss, I am starting to see the justificaiton of this. Can the authors clarify whether a new environment is sampled each time in the outer loop? This is not mentioned in algorithm 1.

R: Yes, we did sample a new environment each time in the outer loop. We've revised this clarification in our paper.

>Q: This is very confusing. Is the hyper-RNN trained on all tasks simultaneously? The paper should make it clear what are the distribution of the training and evaluation tasks and how are they sampled in the outer loop.

R: We train different tasks (i.e. reaching, stacking...etc.) sequentially, not simultaneously. The training and evaluation task distributions are handled by CausalWorld. Take task "Pushing" as an example: for each outer loop, we use CausalWorld to generate a task with randomly sampled new goal shapes from a goal shape family.

We've revised our draft accordingly.
